The signing table had become a small battlefield by the second hour.

Not because anything had actually gone wrong.

The launch event for DDD: Dark Night Recollections was going extremely well. The bookstore had sold through the first stack before lunch, the replacement cartons were already open behind the counter, and E.Red had been smiling so consistently that the muscles around her cheeks had begun to hurt.

The problem stood approximately three feet to her left.

L.Night wore black from collar to ankle, arms folded, expression half asleep.

She was technically E.Red's manager.

Technically.

In practice, she had spent most of the afternoon functioning as a highly selective security system.

"Could I get a photo too?" a man asked after E.Red signed his copy.

"Of course."

E.Red turned toward him with the polished smile she'd perfected over several book launches.

The man stepped around the corner of the table.

L.Night's eyes moved.

He took another step.

L.Night unfolded her arms.

"Here is fine."

The man stopped.

There was still a perfectly respectable distance between him and E.Red.

Apparently not respectable enough.

"Oh." He looked at the floor marker beside him. "Right."

E.Red bit the inside of her cheek.

The photograph was taken.

The man thanked her, collected his novel, and left.

Only then did E.Red glance sideways.

"L.Night."

"What?"

"You know they're allowed to stand next to me."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"Yes."

"Then why did you look at him like he was about to appear in chapter fourteen?"

L.Night frowned.

"Which one was chapter fourteen?"

"The basement."

"Oh."

A pause.

"He wasn't that suspicious."

E.Red stared at her.

That was apparently a compliment.

The absurdity was that L.Night had been like this long before either of them had jobs worth putting on business cards.

They had met in a university fiction club, where E.Red wrote elegant little stories about women with secrets and L.Night mostly sat in the corner reading them with the expression of someone inspecting evidence.

Somewhere between graduation, E.Red getting formally signed by a publisher, and her first few public appearances, L.Night had naturally become the person handling her schedule.

Then her luggage.

Then difficult event organizers.

Then men who leaned too close.

Then, somehow, her apartment.

They lived together now.

That fact was considerably easier to explain than their relationship.

They had kissed.

They had slept in the same bed.

They had crossed enough other boundaries that E.Red privately considered the phrase just friends an insult to both language and basic observational skills.

They had never actually decided what they were.

L.Night seemed perfectly comfortable with this arrangement.

E.Red was less certain.

"Next, please."

Another reader approached.

This time, a woman.

L.Night immediately returned to looking bored.

E.Red lowered her head and signed the title page.

"Thank you for coming."

"I love your books," the reader said. "Especially the romance."

"Really? Thank you."

"The horror too, obviously. But the women always feel so..."

She hesitated.

E.Red smiled. "Dangerously attached?"

"Yes!"

"That's intentional."

From beside her came a quiet snort.

E.Red's pen stopped.

She looked up.

L.Night was studying the ceiling.

Interesting.

By the time the signing finally ended, E.Red's wrist hurt, L.Night had silently intimidated at least seven men, and the bookstore staff had given both of them complimentary coffee vouchers as though compensating them for surviving a natural disaster.

They used them at a café two streets away.

E.Red placed DDD: Dark Night Recollections between them on the little round table.

L.Night placed her iced coffee beside it and immediately looked out the window.

"So," E.Red said. "Chapter nine."

"Mm."

"What did you think?"

"It was good."

"That's all?"

"Yes."

"The protagonist discovers that her girlfriend has been secretly reconstructing every deleted message from their relationship for three years."

"Yes."

"And?"

L.Night took a sip.

"Creepy."

E.Red narrowed her eyes. "It's a psychological thriller."

"I noticed."

"The emotional point is that she can't distinguish devotion from surveillance anymore."

"Mm."

"And the romance is supposed to make that ambiguity worse."

"Sure."

E.Red slowly put her chin in her palm.

L.Night was no longer even pretending to look at the book.

Her attention had drifted toward a dog tied outside the convenience store across the street.

This was offensive.

Not because L.Night disliked fiction. Quite the opposite. She read an unreasonable amount of it.

But E.Red knew exactly what her problem was.

"L.Night."

"Hm?"

"Are you listening?"

"Yes."

"What did I just say?"

L.Night looked back at her.

Silence.

E.Red smiled.

"You weren't."

"I was."

"Repeat it."

"...Surveillance."

"Wonderful. My manager has retained one noun."

L.Night sighed and finally leaned back toward the table. "I read the whole thing."

"I know you did."

"I liked it."

"I know."

"So?"

"So you're sitting here thinking about something else."

That produced the smallest change in L.Night's face.

E.Red knew her too well.

She leaned forward.

"What are you thinking about?"

"Nothing."

"Me?"

"No."

Too fast.

E.Red's smile widened.

L.Night looked away again.

"Oh."

"Don't."

"I haven't done anything."

"You made that face."

"What face?"

"That one."

E.Red reached across the table and gently caught the sleeve at L.Night's wrist.

L.Night looked down at her fingers.

E.Red didn't let go.

"Were you jealous?"

"No."

"Seven men."

"What?"

"You nearly executed seven men with eye contact today."

"One of them put his hand on your chair."

"It was a chair."

"It was your chair."

E.Red stared at her for two seconds.

Then she laughed.

L.Night's brow tightened. "What's funny?"

"You."

"I refuse."

"That's not even an answer."

"It is now."

E.Red's thumb idly brushed the fabric over L.Night's wrist.

The teasing softened without disappearing.

"You know," she said, "for someone who has never formally agreed to be my girlfriend, you're remarkably territorial."

L.Night froze.

There.

E.Red almost felt cruel for enjoying it.

Almost.

She leaned closer over the table.

"So what exactly are you protecting?"

L.Night stared at her.

E.Red waited.

Five seconds.

Ten.

Then L.Night looked down at the hand still holding her sleeve.

"You."

E.Red's smile stopped.

L.Night picked up her coffee with her free hand.

"And the book," she added.

E.Red's eyes narrowed.

"The book?"

"Limited signed stock."

"You horrible woman."

"It's valuable."

E.Red kicked her lightly under the table.

L.Night's knee bumped against hers.

Neither moved away.

Outside, pedestrians passed the café windows. Inside, the espresso machine hissed, cups knocked softly against saucers, and DDD: Dark Night Recollections remained abandoned between them despite supposedly being the entire reason they had come here.

E.Red looked down at their knees touching beneath the table.

Then at her own hand, still wrapped around L.Night's sleeve.

Then back at L.Night.

"You know what's irritating?"

"What?"

"We came here to discuss my novel."

"Mm."

"And somehow you're still more distracting than the serial stalker I wrote."

L.Night took another sip.

"Skill issue."

E.Red stared at her in disbelief.

Then she kicked her again.

Across the city, C.Curo was sitting in a way no ergonomic-chair manufacturer had ever intended.

Both legs were folded onto the seat, knees drawn loosely toward her chest, silver-gray hair falling over one shoulder as she gave the latest chapter one final inspection.

The room around her was perfectly ordinary. A large monitor. Mechanical keyboard. Half-finished drink. Expensive gaming-style ergonomic chair. A neatly organized desk with absolutely nothing on it suggesting that the woman sitting there routinely produced material capable of ruining a reader's appetite for several days.

C.Curo scrolled to the bottom.

One last typo.

Fixed.

She leaned back.

"Publish."

Click.

The chapter went live.

If online fiction came with censorship mosaics, roughly eighty percent of C.Curo's work would probably have been covered by them.

Sex. Violence. Blood. Grotesque imagery. Heresy. Obsessions that started as romance and ended somewhere between psychological horror and a criminal investigation.

Sometimes all in the same chapter.

It was difficult to reconcile those stories with their author.

C.Curo herself was a striking silver-gray-haired woman who looked entirely capable of appearing in public without causing anyone concern. Beautiful, composed, casually stylish. The kind of person a stranger might assume worked in fashion, design, or some expensive creative industry.

Not someone who could stare at a blank document for three seconds and casually type a scene that made thousands of readers wonder whether they should continue eating dinner.

She knew her appearance would attract attention.

That was precisely why no one got to see it.

C.Curo had never shown her face publicly.

No signing events. No author photographs. No casual selfies with strategically hidden backgrounds. She kept personal accounts separate, stripped identifying information from anything connected to her pen name, and treated every tiny piece of metadata as though an obsessive stranger might eventually inspect it.

It wasn't paranoia without precedent.

Too many readers had reported her work over the years because they'd discovered, apparently with great surprise, that the author famous for extreme fiction wrote extreme fiction.

Some had gone beyond complaints.

After that, C.Curo had become meticulous.

Let them hate the stories.

They didn't need to know where the author bought groceries.

With the new chapter safely released into the wild, she opened another tab.

"Let's see..."

E.Red's new book.

C.Curo's posture shifted slightly.

"DDD: Dark Night Recollections..."

She had always liked E.Red's work.

The contrast with her own was almost absurd.

C.Curo wrote love as contamination. As ritual. As fixation pushed so far beyond ordinary human behavior that affection became indistinguishable from worship, possession, mutilation, or madness.

E.Red could put romance inside a nightmare and somehow make it refreshing.

To C.Curo, her love stories were like mint-lemon candy in the middle of a horror novel: sweet without becoming cloying, feminine without becoming fragile. There was always just enough softness to make the darkness around it feel darker.

C.Curo clicked the purchase button.

No hesitation.

She owned every one of E.Red's books.

A few seconds later, the order confirmation appeared.

"Mm."

Satisfied, she wandered over to E.Red's public social feed.

Photos from today's signing event had already begun appearing.

Stacks of books.

A promotional display.

E.Red behind the signing table, smiling toward the camera.

C.Curo stopped scrolling.

"..."

She enlarged the photo.

E.Red really was beautiful.

C.Curo knew that already. Anyone who followed the author's public appearances knew it. Her looks were practically part of the publisher's marketing strategy at this point.

Still.

C.Curo stared a little longer than necessary.

Then moved to the next photo.

E.Red signing a book.

Next.

E.Red holding the new release beside her face.

Next.

E.Red laughing at something outside the frame.

C.Curo's thumb slowed against the mouse wheel.

"Hm."

Next.

E.Red again.

And beside her—

Purple hair.

C.Curo's expression changed immediately.

She scrolled back.

There.

That woman.

L.Night.

C.Curo frowned.

"It's her."

She knew the name only from what could be gathered publicly. Manager. Event companion. Frequently nearby. Often photographed at E.Red's appearances despite looking as though she'd rather be anywhere else.

C.Curo moved to another photograph.

There she was again.

Another.

Again.

Always near E.Red.

C.Curo's frown deepened.

For some reason, seeing that purple-haired woman standing beside E.Red irritated her.

It was an irrational reaction.

C.Curo knew that.

She had never met E.Red.

She had never met L.Night.

E.Red did not know she existed beyond, perhaps, recognizing the pen name of another moderately well-known online writer—assuming she had ever encountered it at all.

There was absolutely no legitimate reason for C.Curo to care who stood beside her at a signing event.

She clicked another photo anyway.

L.Night was looking toward someone outside the frame while E.Red signed a book.

C.Curo narrowed her eyes.

Another photo.

L.Night leaning toward E.Red, apparently saying something.

C.Curo's mouth flattened.

"..."

No.

That wasn't just professional.

She couldn't prove it.

There was no obvious embrace. No public kiss. No announcement. Nothing that would survive even the most generous definition of evidence.

But C.Curo wrote obsession for fun.

She spent an unreasonable portion of her life constructing characters who could identify an affair from the placement of two drinking glasses.

And something about the distance between those two women bothered her.

Too natural.

Too familiar.

L.Night wasn't standing beside E.Red like an employee waiting for instructions.

She was standing there like she belonged there.

C.Curo slowly unfolded one leg from the chair.

"What are you to her...?"

The question came out quieter than intended.

She stared at the photograph.

Then immediately frowned at herself.

"What?"

Why was she interrogating a photograph?

C.Curo closed it.

Two seconds passed.

She reopened it.

"...Hm."

Her new chapter had been online for less than ten minutes.

Already, comments were probably arriving to accuse her of corrupting literature, morality, romance, anatomy, religion, or all five simultaneously.

C.Curo ignored them.

She was busy investigating something far more personally offensive.

E.Red's manager.

C.Curo dealt with her irritation in the mature, emotionally responsible manner expected of a grown woman.

She wrote horror about it.

Not a long story. Just a short piece.

A harmless little act of revenge against a purple-haired stranger who had never spoken to her, harmed her, or demonstrated any awareness that C.Curo existed.

The premise came quickly.

A novelist fell in love with her manager.

The novelist was talented, successful, and hopelessly trusting. Her manager appeared lazy and protective at first, always standing between her and troublesome readers, handling inconvenient people, deciding which invitations were worth accepting.

Helpful.

Dependable.

Comforting.

Until the protection began narrowing her world.

The manager filtered her messages.

Then her friends.

Then her schedule.

Then the places she was allowed to visit alone.

Every controlling act came wrapped in such plausible concern that the novelist kept accepting one more restriction, then another, until she finally noticed that she hadn't made a meaningful decision for herself in months.

By then, leaving was no longer simple.

C.Curo wrote the ending in less than three hundred words.

Short.

Clinical.

Sick enough that even she paused after typing the final sentence.

"...Good."

Publish.

There.

Petty satisfaction achieved.

She never mentioned E.Red. She never described L.Night. She didn't even give the characters remotely similar appearances.

As far as anyone else was concerned, it was simply another C.Curo story in which love began somewhere recognizable and then quietly crawled into a place where healthy human behavior went to die.

A few days later, C.Curo was checking the comments beneath it.

Most were predictable.

Some praised the ending.

Some demanded an explanation.

One reader informed her that she needed psychiatric evaluation.

C.Curo gave that one a like.

Then a particular username caught her attention.

RRR:

"I should show this to my manager. This is hilarious."

C.Curo stopped.

Her hand left the mouse.

"What?"

She stared at the comment.

Manager.

Of all possible words.

Her mind made the connection so quickly that she was annoyed with herself for it.

E.Red.

No.

That was ridiculous.

DDD Publishing had plenty of signed writers. Plenty of people had managers. Plenty of readers had managers too, depending on their professions.

C.Curo clicked the profile.

Private.

Almost empty.

No identifying photograph.

No useful biography.

Nothing.

"Hm."

She returned to the comment.

Then, against better judgment, clicked Reply.

Her public author persona was nothing like the woman currently curled up in an ergonomic chair investigating a stranger's punctuation.

Online, C.Curo was cold.

Sparse.

Almost ceremonial.

Given the material she published, readers had gradually constructed an image of her as something between an aloof intellectual and a perfectly reasonable cult leader.

C.Curo had never bothered correcting them.

She typed:

"You have a manager? Someone important?"

The reply came sooner than expected.

RRR:

"Not important. Just need one for work~"

C.Curo went completely still.

"..."

The tilde.

She stared at it.

That proved nothing.

Absolutely nothing.

Millions of people used tildes.

Probably.

But E.Red used them often in her public posts, particularly when answering readers casually. C.Curo had seen enough of those replies to recognize the rhythm.

She opened E.Red's social feed in another tab.

Scrolled.

A reply to a reader.

"Thank you for coming today~"

Another.

"I'll try not to make the next one too scary~"

Another.

"That's a secret~"

C.Curo slowly returned to RRR.

"Not important. Just need one for work~"

"..."

Her eyes narrowed.

Had the platform recommended the story to E.Red?

That was possible.

Their audiences overlapped. Both wrote horror, although C.Curo's definition of horror occasionally seemed to include crimes against human civilization. Recommendation algorithms weren't exactly known for respecting professional boundaries.

Maybe E.Red had found it.

Maybe she'd read it.

Maybe this was her private account.

Which meant—

C.Curo looked at her own story title.

Then remembered precisely what she had written.

An innocent novelist.

Her manager.

Possessiveness disguised as protection.

A progressively controlling relationship.

That ending.

C.Curo slowly covered her mouth with one hand.

"...No."

If RRR really was E.Red, then C.Curo had accidentally delivered her petty revenge fantasy directly to its inspiration.

Worse—

E.Red had called it hilarious.

C.Curo stared at the screen.

"What kind of reaction is that?"

She opened RRR's profile again as though useful personal information might spontaneously materialize through intimidation.

Nothing.

Perhaps it was simply a reader imitating E.Red's writing habits.

Fans did that.

Didn't they?

C.Curo leaned closer.

RRR.

Three R's.

Red?

No. Too obvious.

Or deliberately obvious because nobody would believe anyone could be that obvious?

Her fingers hovered over the keyboard.

She could ask another question.

Something innocuous.

Something that might reveal whether RRR worked in publishing.

But that would be strange.

C.Curo frowned.

She was an anonymous extreme-horror writer interrogating an equally anonymous commenter because the commenter used a tilde.

There were limits.

She sat back.

Five seconds later, she leaned forward again.

Typed a reply.

Deleted it.

Typed another.

Deleted that too.

Finally:

"Your manager isn't controlling?"

She stared at the sentence.

Too obvious.

Delete.

"Do you like your manager?"

Worse.

Delete.

"How long have you worked together?"

Absolutely not.

Delete.

C.Curo crossed her arms.

"...Hmph."

The cult leader had encountered her greatest natural enemy.

A private account with insufficient information.

C.Curo eventually decided to solve the problem using the skill set in which she had the most confidence.

She wrote another story.

This time, she was going fishing.

The setting was a fictional zombie apocalypse.

Civilization had collapsed. Governments were gone, cities had become concrete feeding grounds, and every surviving human had been reduced to a collection of practical questions.

Where was the next safe shelter?

How much ammunition remained?

Was that water drinkable?

Had the woman beside you been bitten?

And, perhaps most importantly—

If the world was ending anyway, exactly how much social restraint was still necessary?

C.Curo's answer was none.

Absolutely none.

Her two protagonists met while trapped inside an abandoned commercial district. Both were competent women, both initially wary, and both gradually realized that surviving together was considerably better than surviving alone.

They shared food.

Protected each other while sleeping.

Patched each other's injuries.

Learned each other's habits.

Admiration became trust. Trust became dependence. Dependence became attraction.

Then C.Curo took every restraint she usually applied to romantic intimacy, folded it neatly, and threw it out the window.

The story became increasingly outrageous.

The protagonists flirted during supply runs. They argued about who had to keep watch because neither trusted the other to remain focused. A supposedly practical body search for bite marks became so suspiciously thorough that even C.Curo paused while writing it.

"It's medically necessary."

She nodded to herself.

Perfectly reasonable.

By the midpoint, they were using the apocalypse as an excuse for practically everything.

There was no society left to judge them.

No workplace policy.

No neighbors.

No etiquette.

No reason to pretend they weren't attracted to each other.

Who was going to complain?

The zombies?

C.Curo pushed it right up against the ceiling without crossing into explicit description, filling the story with shameless proximity, suggestive jokes, reckless kisses, hands lingering where they probably didn't need to, and two women behaving as though the end of civilization had merely liberated them from embarrassment.

Then came the scene that C.Curo privately considered her masterpiece.

The protagonists had barricaded themselves inside a convenience store.

Outside the glass storefront, zombies pressed against one another in a grotesque wall of bodies, palms smearing the windows as they stared hungrily at the two living women inside.

The protagonists were exhausted.

There were no chairs.

There was, however, one unfortunate woman on the floor who was definitely never getting back up.

One protagonist looked down.

Then at the other woman.

Then back down.

"Seat?"

"Seat."

They sat.

On her.

The zombies watched from outside as though witnessing the most confusing cooking program ever produced.

The women, meanwhile, proceeded to flirt.

One protagonist rested against the other's shoulder.

The other casually slipped an arm around her waist.

Beneath them, the deceased stranger fulfilled her final contribution to human civilization by functioning as furniture.

C.Curo wrote the entire exchange with a perfectly straight face.

The fact that all three people in the scene were women somehow made the image even more absurd.

Two living women flirting shamelessly.
